newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Air plan wins support from holdout union.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Air plan wins support from holdout union.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp. Chief Executive Kevin Benson will begin selling the ailing carrier's survival plan to international creditors on Saturday with all but one of its unions supporting the package.

The Canadian Union of Public Employees, which represents 2,700 flight attendants at Canadian, said on Friday it would urge its members to support the life-support strategy in a Dec. 7 vote after earlier this week rejecting it because of its wage cut provisions.

Public employees union President Judy Darcy said union leaders agreed to sign on after British Columbia Premier Glen Clark, in an early morning meeting, offered to increase the province's contribution to the carrier's financial restructuring package by C$3.1 million ($2.3 million).
"We will be recommending acceptance to our membership," Darcy said in an interview.

British Columbia's 11th-hour move will mean workers earning less than C$25,000 ($18,750) a year will not be forced to take reductions in pay. The new earnings threshold compares with a previous level of C$23,000 ($17,250) set when the governments of Canada, Alberta and British Columbia agreed to concessions earlier on Tuesday.

Under the package, cobbled together in marathon meetings with all parties over the past two weeks in Vancouver, British Columbia, employee wage concessions would total C$31.9 million ($23.9 million) per year for four years and government tax breaks and other savings would be C$38.1 million ($$8.6 million).

The plan also includes major route restructurings and a call for a reduction of C$48 million ($36 million) per year in management and computer fees paid to 33-percent owner AMR Corp., the parent of American Airlines.
The strategy envisages a total four-year addition to Canadian's bottom line of C$720 million ($540 million).

Benson, set to start a two-week series of meetings with creditors around the world on Saturday to appeal for time to make payment obligations, said Friday that the day's developments helped it gain the confidence of more than 70 lenders and aircraft lessors.
"I think they will be delighted to hear this morning's news. I think we're in good standing," he told a news conference.
A number of Canadian's creditors had already given it a moratorium on payments while it completed its life-support proposal, Benson said.
The Calgary, Alberta-based carrier, striving to avert financial failure, owes C$2.8 billion ($2.1 billion) including equipment leases.

Benson stressed, however, that the restructuring package still required support from all six unions for its various pieces to fall into place. The powerful Canadian Auto Workers union, which represents 3,700 of Canadian's 16,400 employees, remained opposed to any wage cuts on Friday.
"We do need the CAW on board and I ask and entreat them again to come on board," he said.

At the news conference, British Columbia's Clark said he was convinced the extra concessions to Canadian employees were necessary, given the impact that Canadian has on his provincial economy and the strategic importance of Vancouver to Canadian and American Airlines as a gateway hub to the rich Asian market.
